title: The Cliffs Notes on Cliffs Notes
summary: Josh and Chuck give a brief overview of Cliffs Notes, the yellow-and-black study guide series. They cover its origin in Jack Cole's Cole's Notes, its founder Clifton Hillegass and his Nebraska Book Company background, the renaming and early sales growth, the 1970s sales dip and cassette version, advertising, the company's later sale and ownership changes, criticism as a cheating aid, the Villanova bookstore incident, competitors such as SparkNotes, Schmoop and Thug Notes, and a listener mail note about Broadway previews.
topics: Cliffs Notes business model and subscription

segments.title: Intro and what Cliffs Notes is
segments.summary: The hosts introduce the episode, clarify the correct spelling of Cliffs Notes, and describe the study aid as a condensed guide to classic books, using The Scarlet Letter as an example.

segments.title: Clifton Hillegass early life and career
segments.summary: Clifton Hillegass is profiled: born in 1918 in Nebraska, studied physics and math, dropped out of graduate school to marry Katherine Galbraith, worked at Long's College Books (later Nebraska Book Company), and served as an Army Air Corps meteorologist in World War Two.

segments.title: Jack Cole's Cole's Notes and the renaming
segments.summary: Hillegass became the American distributor of Jack Cole's condensed pamphlets in Toronto, called Cole's Notes. Hillegass took out a loan, printed 33,000 copies, and within the first year renamed them Cliffs Notes, and the hosts discuss whether this was unethical.

segments.title: Early sales and the company's growth
segments.summary: Early sales reached 58,000 copies by the end of 1958. Hillegass quit the Nebraska Book Company job by 1964, changed the name spelling in the 1960s, and divorced and remarried in 1966. The hosts also discuss the stepchildren from the remarriage.

segments.title: Writing approach, branding and advertising
segments.summary: Hillegass hired literature teachers, then graduate students, because teachers knew the books too deeply. The iconic yellow and black design and advertising in Playboy, Seventeen, and college newspapers helped the brand become iconic. Hillegass held about 80 percent of the market for literature guides.

segments.title: Criticism of dated content and 1970s sales dip
segments.summary: The guides were criticized as dated and were updated over time. Around 1969 the classics fell out of favor, pass/fail grading reduced demand, and sales dropped from 2.8 million to 1.8 million units until the mid-1970s.

segments.title: Cliffs Notes cassettes and audiobooks tangent
segments.summary: Cliffs Notes released a cassette version for about six months that did not sell well. The hosts discuss the history of audiobooks starting in 1932 with the American Foundation for the Blind, the Walkman, and personal music players.

segments.title: Hillegass retirement, philanthropy and sale to IDG Books
segments.summary: Hillegass donated profits to Nebraska organizations and supported the Museum of Nebraska Art. He stepped down as president at 65 in 1983 but stayed on as board head. In 1999 at 81 he sold the company to IDG Books for about 14 million dollars and died a couple of years later at 83.

segments.title: Later ownership changes
segments.summary: John Wiley and Sons bought the brand in 2001 and changed the name to CliffsNotes. Houghton Mifflin Harcourt bought it in 2012 and Course Hero bought it in 2021.

segments.title: Sponsor break
segments.summary: Break between segments, with a brief reference to buying the Scarlet Letter pamphlet and a mention of the free website.

segments.title: Free website and subscription model
segments.summary: The Cliffs Notes website offers much free content, with a subscription of about nine dollars a month or thirty six dollars a year for deeper guides and PDFs. The hosts compare the free Scarlet Letter materials to the paid tier and speculate about the business model and course Hero.

segments.title: Cheating debate and Villanova bookstore incident
segments.summary: Hillegass's note at the front of each guide said there are no shortcuts to literature. Teachers sometimes recommended or used the guides. In 1997 Villanova removed Cliffs Notes from its bookstore, and the company ran a newspaper ad calling it censorship.

segments.title: Is it bad to use study guides? Reading the classics
segments.summary: The hosts debate whether reading the book itself matters, citing a University of Kentucky literature scholar's idea of the labor of witnessing. Chuck plans to read The Scarlet Letter, and Josh discusses Moby-Dick and a book he has not read.

segments.title: Competitors and parodies
segments.summary: SparkNotes became a major competitor around 1999 and Schmoop appeared in 2008. Thug Notes, a YouTube series by Greg Edwards, summarizes books in about five minutes, and the hosts discuss its Scarlet Letter episode.

segments.title: Listener mail on Broadway previews
segments.summary: Listener Reagan, a theatrical costume designer, explains how Broadway previews work, including changes to lines, music, staging, and the freezing of the show before critics attend. The hosts thank her.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts give the email address for listener mail and sign off.
